questions.question: For a series of functions $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$, what are its partial sums?
options: $S_N(x) = f_N(x)$
$S_N(x) = \sum_{n = N}^{\infty} f_n(x)$
$S_N(x) = f_1(x)f_2(x)\cdots f_N(x)$

questions.question: When do we say that $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ converges to $f$ on $X$?
options: When the partial sums $S_N$ converge to $f$ pointwise or uniformly on $X$.
When each single term $f_n(x)$ converges to $f(x)$ as $n\to\infty$, for each point $x\in X$.
When the terms satisfy $f_n(x)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, for every $x\in X$.
When the partial sums $S_N$ are uniformly bounded on $X$, for all $N$.

questions.question: Which series of functions fails to converge at some point of $(-1,1)$?
options: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x}{n^2}$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x^n}n$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(nx)$

questions.question: Why is uniform convergence stronger than pointwise convergence for a series of functions?
options: Each point may use an unrelated bound with no common control.
Only the first term is checked.
The same tail bound must work for all points in the domain.
The functions must all be constant.

questions.question: What does the notation $f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n(x)$ mean?
options: The partial sums converge to the function $f$ at the relevant points.
The individual terms $f_n(x)$ converge to $f(x)$ at the relevant points.
The partial sums $S_N(x)$ equal $f(x)$ exactly, for all large enough $N$.
The series converges uniformly to $f$ on the whole of $X$.

questions.question: On a finite closed interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, which condition is sufficient for term-by-term integration?
options: Pointwise convergence of the series together with Riemann integrability of the terms.
Uniform convergence of the terms $f_n$ to $0$ together with their Riemann integrability.
Uniform convergence of the series together with Riemann integrability of the terms.
Absolute convergence of $\sum f_n(x)$ at every point, with each $f_n$ continuous.

questions.question: Let $X=[a,b]$ with finite $a<b$. If $f_n$ are Riemann integrable and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n$ converges uniformly on $X$, which formula is supported?
options: $\int_X\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$
$\int_X\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_X f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n'(x)$
$\int_X\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_X f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

questions.question: The series $f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sin(nx)/n^2$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$. Which statement about differentiating it term by term on an interval containing $0$ is correct?
options: Not justified by this alone: the theorem needs uniform convergence of the derivative series $\sum_n\cos(nx)/n$, which diverges at $x=0$.
Justified: uniform convergence of $\sum_n\sin(nx)/n^2$ itself gives $f'(x)=\sum_n\cos(nx)/n$ on the interval.
Justified: each term is differentiable, and a sum of differentiable functions can always be differentiated term by term.
Justified: $f'(x)=\sum_n\cos(nx)/n^2$, because differentiating does not change the factor $1/n^2$.

questions.question: The series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n/n!$ converges to $\mathrm{e}^x$ for every real $x$. On which sets does it converge uniformly?
options: On every bounded interval $[-R,R]$, but not on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
On all of $\mathbb{R}$, because it converges at every point of $\mathbb{R}$.
On no interval, because the terms $x^n/n!$ are unbounded on $\mathbb{R}$.
Only on $[-1,1]$, where $|x^n/n!|\le1/n!$ gives a convergent bound.

questions.question: For $n=0,1,2,\dots$ let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{(1+x^2)^n}$ on $\mathbb{R}$; every $f_n$ is continuous. What is the pointwise sum $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f_n(x)$?
options: $f(x)=1+x^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$
$f(x)=1+x^2$ for $x\ne0$, while the series diverges at $x=0$
$f(x)=1$ for $x\ne0$, and $f(0)=0$

questions.question: Term-by-term integration $\int_a^b\sum_{n}f_n=\sum_{n}\int_a^b f_n$ is guaranteed for a uniformly convergent series of Riemann-integrable functions on a finite interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$. Why does the argument need the interval to be finite?
options: A series of functions cannot converge uniformly on an unbounded interval, so the hypothesis could never hold there.
On a finite interval each $f_n$ is bounded, and bounded terms may be integrated term by term even without uniform convergence.
If $|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\varepsilon$ on $[a,b]$, the integrals of $f$ and $S_N$ differ by at most $(b-a)\varepsilon$, which tends to $0$.
Sums and improper integrals over unbounded intervals can never be interchanged, so the theorem has to exclude them.
